Use this reference to look up event schemas, configuration options, JSON input/output formats, and advanced features like async hooks, HTTP hooks, and MCP tool hooks. If you're setting up hooks for the first time, start with the [guide](/en/hooks-guide) instead. 14→ 15→## Hook lifecycle 16→ 17→Hooks fire at specific points during a Claude Code session. When an event fires and a matcher matches, Claude Code passes JSON context about the event to your hook handler. For command hooks, input arrives on stdin. For HTTP hooks, it arrives as the POST request body. Your handler can then inspect the input, take action, and optionally return a decision. Some events fire once per session, while others fire repeatedly inside the agentic loop: 18→ 19→
20→ 21→ 22→ 23→
24→ 25→The table below summarizes when each event fires. The [Hook events](#hook-events) section documents the full input schema and decision control options for each one. 26→ 27→| Event | When it fires | 28→| :------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 29→| `SessionStart` | When a session begins or resumes | 30→| `UserPromptSubmit` | When you submit a prompt, before Claude processes it | 31→| `PreToolUse` | Before a tool call executes. Can block it | 32→| `PermissionRequest` | When a permission dialog appears | 33→| `PostToolUse` | After a tool call succeeds | 34→| `PostToolUseFailure` | After a tool call fails | 35→| `Notification` | When Claude Code sends a notification | 36→| `SubagentStart` | When a subagent is spawned | 37→| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent finishes | 38→| `Stop` | When Claude finishes responding | 39→| `TeammateIdle` | When an [agent team](/en/agent-teams) teammate is about to go idle | 40→| `TaskCompleted` | When a task is being marked as completed | 41→| `ConfigChange` | When a configuration file changes during a session | 42→| `WorktreeCreate` | When a worktree is being created via `--worktree` or `isolation: "worktree"`. Replaces default git behavior | 43→| `WorktreeRemove` | When a worktree is being removed, either at session exit or when a subagent finishes | 44→| `PreCompact` | Before context compaction | 45→| `SessionEnd` | When a session terminates | 46→ 47→### How a hook resolves 48→ 49→To see how these pieces fit together, consider this `PreToolUse` hook that blocks destructive shell commands. The hook runs `block-rm.sh` before every Bash tool call: 50→ 51→```json theme={null} 52→{ 53→ "hooks": { 54→ "PreToolUse": [ 55→ { 56→ "matcher": "Bash", 57→ "hooks": [ 58→ { 59→ "type": "command", 60→ "command": ".claude/hooks/block-rm.sh" 61→ } 62→ ] 63→ } 64→ ] 65→ } 66→} 67→``` 68→ 69→The script reads the JSON input from stdin, extracts the command, and returns a `permissionDecision` of `"deny"` if it contains `rm -rf`: 70→ 71→```bash theme={null} 72→#!/bin/bash 73→# .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh 74→COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command') 75→ 76→if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then 77→ jq -n '{ 78→ hookSpecificOutput: { 79→ hookEventName: "PreToolUse", 80→ permissionDecision: "deny", 81→ permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive command blocked by hook" 82→ } 83→ }' 84→else 85→ exit 0 # allow the command 86→fi 87→``` 88→ 89→Now suppose Claude Code decides to run `Bash "rm -rf /tmp/build"`. Here's what happens: 90→ 91→ 92→ 93→ 94→ 95→ 96→ 97→ The `PreToolUse` event fires. Claude Code sends the tool input as JSON on stdin to the hook: 98→ 99→ ```json theme={null} 100→ { "tool_name": "Bash", "tool_input": { "command": "rm -rf /tmp/build" }, ... } 101→ ``` 102→ 103→ 104→ 105→ The matcher `"Bash"` matches the tool name, so `block-rm.sh` runs. If you omit the matcher or use `"*"`, the hook runs on every occurrence of the event. Hooks only skip when a matcher is defined and doesn't match. 106→ 107→ 108→ 109→ The script extracts `"rm -rf /tmp/build"` from the input and finds `rm -rf`, so it prints a decision to stdout: 110→ 111→ ```json theme={null} 112→ { 113→ "hookSpecificOutput": { 114→ "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", 115→ "permissionDecision": "deny", 116→ "permissionDecisionReason": "Destructive command blocked by hook" 117→ } 118→ } 119→ ``` 120→ 121→ If the command had been safe (like `npm test`), the script would hit `exit 0` instead, which tells Claude Code to allow the tool call with no further action. 122→ 123→ 124→ 125→ Claude Code reads the JSON decision, blocks the tool call, and shows Claude the reason. 126→ 127→ 128→ 129→The [Configuration](#configuration) section below documents the full schema, and each [hook event](#hook-events) section documents what input your command receives and what output it can return. 130→ 131→## Configuration 132→ 133→Hooks are defined in JSON settings files. The configuration has three levels of nesting: 134→ 135→1. Choose a [hook event](#hook-events) to respond to, like `PreToolUse` or `Stop` 136→2. Add a [matcher group](#matcher-patterns) to filter when it fires, like "only for the Bash tool" 137→3. Define one or more [hook handlers](#hook-handler-fields) to run when matched 138→ 139→See [How a hook resolves](#how-a-hook-resolves) above for a complete walkthrough with an annotated example. 140→ 141→ 142→ This page uses specific terms for each level: **hook event** for the lifecycle point, **matcher group** for the filter, and **hook handler** for the shell command, HTTP endpoint, prompt, or agent that runs. "Hook" on its own refers to the general feature. 143→ 144→ 145→### Hook locations 146→ 147→Where you define a hook determines its scope: 148→ 149→| Location | Scope | Shareable | 150→| :--------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------- | :--------------------------------- | 151→| `~/.claude/settings.json` | All your projects | No, local to your machine | 152→| `.claude/settings.json` | Single project | Yes, can be committed to the repo | 153→| `.claude/settings.local.json` | Single project | No, gitignored | 154→| Managed policy settings | Organization-wide | Yes, admin-controlled | 155→| [Plugin](/en/plugins) `hooks/hooks.json` | When plugin is enabled | Yes, bundled with the plugin | 156→| [Skill](/en/skills) or [agent](/en/sub-agents) frontmatter | While the component is active | Yes, defined in the component file | 157→ 158→For details on settings file resolution, see [settings](/en/settings). Enterprise administrators can use `allowManagedHooksOnly` to block user, project, and plugin hooks. See [Hook configuration](/en/settings#hook-configuration). 159→ 160→### Matcher patterns 161→ 162→The `matcher` field is a regex string that filters when hooks fire. Use `"*"`, `""`, or omit `matcher` entirely to match all occurrences. Each event type matches on a different field: 163→ 164→| Event | What the matcher filters | Example matcher values | 165→| :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------ | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 166→| `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionRequest` | tool name | `Bash`, `Edit\|Write`, `mcp__.*` | 167→| `SessionStart` | how the session started | `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, `compact` | 168→| `SessionEnd` | why the session ended | `clear`, `logout`, `prompt_input_exit`, `bypass_permissions_disabled`, `other` | 169→| `Notification` | notification type | `permission_prompt`, `idle_prompt`, `auth_success`, `elicitation_dialog` | 170→| `SubagentStart` | agent type | `Bash`, `Explore`, `Plan`, or custom agent names | 171→| `PreCompact` | what triggered compaction | `manual`, `auto` | 172→| `SubagentStop` | agent type | same values as `SubagentStart` | 173→| `ConfigChange` | configuration source | `user_settings`, `project_settings`, `local_settings`, `policy_settings`, `skills` | 174→| `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCompleted`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove` | no matcher support | always fires on every occurrence | 175→ 176→The matcher is a regex, so `Edit|Write` matches either tool and `Notebook.*` matches any tool starting with Notebook. The matcher runs against a field from the [JSON input](#hook-input-and-output) that Claude Code sends to your hook on stdin. For tool events, that field is `tool_name`. Each [hook event](#hook-events) section lists the full set of matcher values and the input schema for that event. 177→ 178→This example runs a linting script only when Claude writes or edits a file: 179→ 180→```json theme={null} 181→{ 182→ "hooks": { 183→ "PostToolUse": [ 184→ { 185→ "matcher": "Edit|Write", 186→ "hooks": [ 187→ { 188→ "type": "command", 189→ "command": "/path/to/lint-check.sh" 190→ } 191→ ] 192→ } 193→ ] 194→ } 195→} 196→``` 197→ 198→`UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCompleted`, `WorktreeCreate`, and `WorktreeRemove` don't support matchers and always fire on every occurrence. If you add a `matcher` field to these events, it is silently ignored. 199→ 200→#### Match MCP tools

The hook runs `block-rm.sh` before every Bash tool call: ```json theme={null} { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/block-rm.sh" } ] } ] } } ``` The script reads the JSON input from stdin, extracts the command, and returns a `permissionDecision` of `"deny"` if it contains `rm -rf`: ```bash theme={null} #!/bin/bash # .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command') if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then jq -n '{ hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: "PreToolUse", permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive command blocked by hook" } }' else exit 0 # allow the command fi ``` Now suppose Claude Code decides to run `Bash "rm -rf /tmp/build"`. Here's what happens: The `PreToolUse` event fires. Claude Code sends the tool input as JSON on stdin to the hook: ```json theme={null} { "tool_name": "Bash", "tool_input": { "command": "rm -rf /tmp/build" }, ... } ``` The matcher `"Bash"` matches the tool name, so `block-rm.sh` runs. If you omit the matcher or use `"*"`, the hook runs on every occurrence of the event. Hooks only skip when a matcher is defined and doesn't match. The script extracts `"rm -rf /tmp/build"` from the input and finds `rm -rf`, so it prints a decision to stdout: ```json theme={null} { "hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": "Destructive command blocked by hook" } } ``` If the command had been safe (like `npm test`), the script would hit `exit 0` instead, which tells Claude Code to allow the tool call with no further action. Claude Code reads the JSON decision, blocks the tool call, and shows Claude the reason. The [Configuration](#configuration) section below documents the full schema, and each [hook event](#hook-events) section documents what input your command receives and what output it can return. ## Configuration Hooks are defined in JSON settings files. The configuration has three levels of nesting: 1. Choose a [hook event](#hook-events) to respond to, like `PreToolUse` or `Stop` 2. Add a [matcher group](#matcher-patterns) to filter when it fires, like "only for the Bash tool" 3. Define one or more [hook handlers](#hook-handler-fields) to run when matched See [How a hook resolves](#how-a-hook-resolves) above for a complete walkthrough with an annotated example. This page uses specific terms for each level: **hook event** for the lifecycle point, **matcher group** for the filter, and **hook handler** for the shell command, HTTP endpoint, prompt, or agent that runs. "Hook" on its own refers to the general feature. ### Hook locations Where you define a hook determines its scope: | Location | Scope | Shareable | | :--------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------- | :--------------------------------- | | `~/.claude/settings.json` | All your projects | No, local to your machine | | `.claude/settings.json` | Single project | Yes, can be committed to the repo | | `.claude/settings.local.json` | Single project | No, gitignored | | Managed policy settings | Organization-wide | Yes, admin-controlled | | [Plugin](/en/plugins) `hooks/hooks.json` | When plugin is enabled | Yes, bundled with the plugin | | [Skill](/en/skills) or [agent](/en/sub-agents) frontmatter | While the component is active | Yes, defined in the component file | For details on settings file resolution, see [settings](/en/settings). Enterprise administrators can use `allowManagedHooksOnly` to block user, project, and plugin hooks. See [Hook configuration](/en/settings#hook-configuration). ### Matcher patterns The `matcher` field is a regex string that filters when hooks fire. Use `"*"`, `""`, or omit `matcher` entirely to match all occurrences. Each event type matches on a different field: | Event | What the matcher filters | Example matcher values | | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------ | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionRequest` | tool name | `Bash`, `Edit\|Write`, `mcp__.*` | | `SessionStart` | how the session started | `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, `compact` | | `SessionEnd` | why the session ended | `clear`, `logout`, `prompt_input_exit`, `bypass_permissions_disabled`, `other` | | `Notification` | notification type | `permission_prompt`, `idle_prompt`, `auth_success`, `elicitation_dialog` | | `SubagentStart` | agent type | `Bash`, `Explore`, `Plan`, or custom agent names | | `PreCompact` | what triggered compaction | `manual`, `auto` | | `SubagentStop` | agent type | same values as `SubagentStart` | | `ConfigChange` | configuration source | `user_settings`, `project_settings`, `local_settings`, `policy_settings`, `skills` | | `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCompleted`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove` | no matcher support | always fires on every occurrence | The matcher is a regex, so `Edit|Write` matches either tool and `Notebook.*` matches any tool starting with Notebook. The matcher runs against a field from the [JSON input](#hook-input-and-output) that Claude Code sends to your hook on stdin. For tool events, that field is `tool_name`. Each [hook event](#hook-events) section lists the full set of matcher values and the input schema for that event. This example runs a linting script only when Claude writes or edits a file: ```json theme={null} { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/lint-check.sh" } ] } ] } } ``` `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCompleted`, `WorktreeCreate`, and `WorktreeRemove` don't support matchers and always fire on every occurrence. If you add a `matcher` field to these events, it is silently ignored. #### Match MCP tools

## Integration Patterns Analysis

### Communication Protocols — Unified stdin/stdout JSON

All three CLIs use a conceptually similar hook communication pattern, but with important differences:

| Aspect | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode |
|--------|-------------|------------|----------|
| **Transport** | stdin → stdout (JSON) | stdin → stdout (JSON) | Function call → return value |
| **Block signal** | Exit 2 OR `permissionDecision: "deny"` | Exit 2 OR `decision: "deny"` | `throw new Error()` |
| **Allow signal** | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Return nothing |
| **Context injection** | `additionalContext` field in hookSpecificOutput | `systemMessage` or `additionalContext` | Modify args or return context |
| **Handler types** | Command, HTTP, Prompt, Agent | Command only | TypeScript/JavaScript function |
| **Timeout default** | 60s | 60s | N/A (sync JS execution) |
| **Async support** | Yes (background hooks with later injection) | No | Yes (async functions) |

**Key Insight for Entire.io:** The Entire.io CLI already implements adapter layers per agent. For Claude Code and Gemini CLI, it writes JSON shell command hooks into `settings.json`. For OpenCode, it generates a TypeScript plugin file at `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. This means the protocol translation is handled by Entire.io — consumers don't need to care about per-CLI differences.

_Source: [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Gemini CLI Hooks Reference](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/reference/), [OpenCode Plugins Docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/)_

### Hook Event Mapping Across CLIs

Entire.io needs to map its 7 lifecycle events to each CLI's event model:

| Entire.io Hook | Claude Code Event | Gemini CLI Event | OpenCode Event |
|----------------|-------------------|------------------|----------------|
| `SessionStart` | `SessionStart` | `SessionStart` | `session.created` |
| `SessionEnd` | `SessionEnd` | `SessionEnd` | `session.idle` or `session.deleted` |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | `UserPromptSubmit` | `BeforeAgent` | `tui.command.execute` |
| `Stop` (checkpoint trigger) | `Stop` | `AfterAgent` | `session.updated` |
| `PreToolUse` (subagent) | `PreToolUse` (matcher: `Agent`) | `BeforeTool` | `tool.execute.before` |
| `PostToolUse` (subagent) | `PostToolUse` (matcher: `Agent`) | `AfterTool` | `tool.execute.after` |
| `PostToolUse[TodoWrite]` | `PostToolUse` (matcher: `TodoWrite`) | `AfterTool` (matcher: `todo`) | `todo.updated` |

**Confidence: HIGH for Claude Code (GA), MEDIUM for Gemini/OpenCode (preview)**

_Source: [Under the Hood article](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/), respective CLI documentation_

### Context Injection Patterns — The Key Integration Point

The most valuable pattern for Cohezion's agent context awareness is **SessionStart context injection**. Each CLI supports injecting context when a session starts:

**Claude Code:**
```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "Context string injected into Claude's system prompt"
  }
}
```
The `additionalContext` is prepended to the first prompt. Non-JSON stdout from SessionStart hooks is also injected directly into context.

**Gemini CLI:**
```json
{
  "systemMessage": "Context injected as system message",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "additionalContext": "Additional context appended to prompt"
  }
}
```
Both `systemMessage` and `additionalContext` are supported. The `source` field in input (`startup|resume|clear`) allows different injection behavior per trigger.

**OpenCode:**
```typescript
export const ContextPlugin = async ({ project }) => ({
  hooks: {
    "session.created": async (input) => {
      // Inject context via custom tool or tui.prompt.append
    },
    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input) => {
      // Inject context that survives compaction
    }
  }
})
```
OpenCode uses `experimental.session.compacting` for context that must survive compaction — critical for persistent session awareness.

_Source: [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Gemini CLI Hooks Reference](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/reference/), [OpenCode Plugins](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/)_

### Entire.io Data Access Patterns

For context injection to work, a SessionStart hook needs to query Entire.io's data. Available CLI commands:

| Command | Output | Use Case |
|---------|--------|----------|
| `entire status` | Active sessions, agent types, token counts | "What's happening now across all agents?" |
| `entire explain --short` | Checkpoint list with session summaries | "What was accomplished in recent sessions?" |
| `entire explain --checkpoint <id> --short` | Single checkpoint summary | "What did session X do?" |
| `entire explain --session <id>` | All checkpoints for a session | "Full history of a specific session" |
| `entire explain --generate` | AI-generated summary (requires Claude CLI) | "Summarize what happened for injection" |

**Performance Characteristics:**
- `entire status`: ~200ms (reads local metadata)
- `entire explain --short`: ~500ms (reads checkpoint branch)
- `entire explain --generate`: 3-10s (calls Claude CLI for AI summary)
- `entire rewind --list`: ~300ms (reads shadow branches)

**Integration Pattern: SessionStart → entire status → format → inject as context**

A shell hook can be shared across Claude Code and Gemini CLI (both use shell commands). OpenCode requires a TypeScript wrapper that shells out to the `entire` binary.

_Source: [Entire CLI Commands](https://docs.entire.io/cli/commands), local testing on this project_

### Cross-Agent Session Visibility Architecture

The core architectural challenge: making each agent aware of what other agents are doing in parallel. The data flow:

```
Agent A (Claude Code) starts session
  └→ Entire hooks capture SessionStart
      └→ Shadow branch created
          └→ Checkpoints accumulate on turns

Agent B (Gemini CLI) starts session
  └→ SessionStart hook fires
      └→ Hook runs: entire status
          └→ Sees Agent A's active session
              └→ Injects: "Claude Code session active on branch X, working on Y"
```

**Conflict Detection Pattern:**
```
SessionStart hook:
  1. Run `entire status` → parse JSON output
  2. Filter for sessions on same branch or touching same files
  3. If overlap detected → inject warning context
  4. If no overlap → inject awareness context (FYI only)
```

**File-Level Conflict Detection (Advanced):**
```
Stop/AfterAgent hook:
  1. Run `entire explain --checkpoint <latest> --short`
  2. Extract files_touched list
  3. Compare against other active sessions' files_touched
  4. If overlap → inject merge-risk warning
```

_Source: Architecture derived from [Entire.io Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts) and [Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/)_

### Bidirectional Traceability Integration

Entire.io's commit trailers create a traceability chain that maps directly to Cohezion's existing BMAD workflow:

```
PRD Requirement (FR-X)
  └→ Epic (Epic 12: Sovereign-Sync Bedrock)
      └→ Story (Story 12.1: JSON-RPC Bridge)
          └→ Sprint Task (implementation)
              └→ Git Commit (feat: add JSON-RPC gateway)
                  └→ Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7
                      └→ Full Session Transcript
                          └→ Prompts, Decisions, Files, Token Cost
```

**Trailer Format:**
```
feat: add JSON-RPC gateway

Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7
Entire-Attribution: 73% agent (146/200 lines)
```

**Querying the chain:**
- From commit → `entire explain --commit <sha>` → session context
- From checkpoint → `entire explain --checkpoint <id>` → files, prompts, tokens
- From session → `entire explain --session <id>` → all checkpoints in session

**Known Limitation:** Squash merges (common in PR workflows) destroy commit trailers, breaking the bidirectional link. This needs a workaround for Cohezion's worktree-based `cz worktree sync` flow.

_Source: [Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts), [Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/)_

### Security Patterns

**Secret Redaction:** Entire.io performs best-effort redaction of API keys, tokens, and credentials when writing to `entire/checkpoints/v1`. However:
- Shadow branches during active sessions may contain unredacted data
- Redaction is pattern-based, not comprehensive
- Public repos expose full session transcripts

**Hook Security:**
- Claude Code: Hooks run with user permissions, outside the Bash tool sandbox
- Gemini CLI: Project-level hooks fingerprinted; warns on changes from git pull
- OpenCode: Plugin hooks don't intercept subagent tool calls (known bug — [Issue #5894](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/5894))

**Recommendation for Cohezion:** Since Cohezion is a private repo with sensitive research data:
1. Use `.entire/settings.local.json` for any API keys in summarization config
2. Review `entire/checkpoints/v1` before pushing to remote
3. Consider `--skip-push-sessions` for sensitive branches

_Source: [GitHub README](https://github.com/entireio/cli), [Entire Configuration](https://docs.entire.io/cli/configuration)_

### Current State Gap Analysis (This Project)

| Component | Expected | Actual | Gap |
|-----------|----------|--------|-----|
| Claude Code hooks | Full lifecycle | **Installed** (6 event types) | None |
| Gemini CLI hooks | Full lifecycle | **Missing** (no `.gemini/settings.json`) | `entire enable --agent gemini` needed |
| OpenCode plugin | TypeScript plugin | **Missing** (no `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`) | `entire enable --agent opencode` needed |
| Context injection | SessionStart hook queries `entire status` | **Not implemented** | Custom hook needed per CLI |
| Cross-session awareness | Agents see each other's work | **Not implemented** | Custom SessionStart hook + formatter |
| Conflict detection | File-level overlap warnings | **Not implemented** | Custom Stop/AfterAgent hook |
| Traceability | Commit trailers → BMAD stories | **Passive** (trailers exist but not queried) | Query integration with sprint status |
| Stuck session cleanup | Automated | **Manual** (15 stuck sessions) | `entire doctor --force` or automated cron |

_Confidence: HIGH — verified against local installation state_

Entire.io is a Git-native observability layer for AI agent sessions. It hooks into both the AI agent and Git itself to capture code generation provenance — prompts, responses, files touched, token usage, tool calls — without polluting your commit history.

### Entire.io Architecture Internals

**Shadow Branches:** During active sessions, Entire creates temporary local branches named `entire/<hash>-<worktree-id>` using go-git plumbing APIs — no checkout, no stash, no visible side effects. Deduplication is automatic via Git's content-addressable storage. Shadow branches are never pushed remotely.

**Checkpoint Metadata Branch:** The orphan branch `entire/checkpoints/v1` stores permanent metadata in a sharded directory structure:
```
entire/checkpoints/v1
└── a3/b2c4d5e6f7/           # 6-byte random checkpoint ID (12 hex chars)
    ├── metadata.json         # summary, attribution, tokens
    ├── 0/
    │   ├── full.jsonl        # complete transcript
    │   ├── prompt.txt        # user prompts
    │   └── context.md
    └── 1/                    # additional sessions if needed
```

**Bidirectional Linking:** Git commit trailers (`Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7`) create traceable links between code commits and session metadata. The `Entire-Attribution` trailer quantifies agent vs. human contributions (e.g., "73% agent (146/200 lines)").

**JSONL Transcript Parsing:** Entire reads the same JSONL files that agents write to disk. The CLI parses transcripts to extract modified files (from `tool_use` blocks), user prompts, token usage, and summaries. No APIs involved — purely filesystem-based parsing.

**Strategies:**
- `manual-commit` (default): Checkpoints created only at Git commit time
- `auto-commit`: Checkpoints after every agent response (finer-grained save points)

**Auto-Summarization:** When enabled (`strategy_options.summarize.enabled`), generates AI summaries at commit time using Claude CLI. Non-blocking failures.

_Source: [How Entire Works Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/), [Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts)_

Seven lifecycle hooks cover the full session:

| Hook Event | Purpose | Trigger |
|------------|---------|---------|
| `SessionStart` | Track session boundary | Agent starts |
| `SessionEnd` | Track session boundary | Agent exits |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | Capture human edits baseline | Before agent processes prompt |
| `Stop` | Trigger checkpoint save | After agent finishes a turn |
| `PreToolUse` | Monitor subagent spawning | Before tool execution |
| `PostToolUse` | Monitor subagent completion | After tool execution |
| `PostToolUse[TodoWrite]` | Capture task state | After todo updates |

Each hook executes shell commands like `entire hooks claude-code stop`. The hook reads agent-specific JSONL from well-known paths (e.g., Claude Code's session logs).

_Source: [Under the Hood article](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/), [Commands Reference](https://docs.entire.io/cli/commands)_

|-------|--------|------------|

lines: +All three CLIs use a conceptually similar hook communication pattern, but with important differences:
+| Aspect | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode |
+| **Transport** | stdin → stdout (JSON) | stdin → stdout (JSON) | Function call → return value |
+| **Block signal** | Exit 2 OR `permissionDecision: "deny"` | Exit 2 OR `decision: "deny"` | `throw new Error()` |
+| **Allow signal** | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Return nothing |
+| **Context injection** | `additionalContext` field in hookSpecificOutput | `systemMessage` or `additionalContext` | Modify args or return context |
+| **Handler types** | Command, HTTP, Prompt, Agent | Command only | TypeScript/JavaScript function |
+| **Async support** | Yes (background hooks with later injection) | No | Yes (async functions) |

+**Key Insight for Entire.io:** The Entire.io CLI already implements adapter layers per agent. For Claude Code and Gemini CLI, it writes JSON shell command hooks into `settings.json`. For OpenCode, it generates a TypeScript plugin file at `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. This means the protocol translation is handled by Entire.io — consumers don't need to care about per-CLI differences.

+_Source: [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Gemini CLI Hooks Reference](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/reference/), [OpenCode Plugins Docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/)_
+Entire.io needs to map its 7 lifecycle events to each CLI's event model:
+| Entire.io Hook | Claude Code Event | Gemini CLI Event | OpenCode Event |
+**Confidence: HIGH for Claude Code (GA), MEDIUM for Gemini/OpenCode (preview)**
+### Context Injection Patterns — The Key Integration Point
+The most valuable pattern for Cohezion's agent context awareness is **SessionStart context injection**. Each CLI supports injecting context when a session starts:
+    "additionalContext": "Context string injected into Claude's system prompt"
+The `additionalContext` is prepended to the first prompt. Non-JSON stdout from SessionStart hooks is also injected directly into context.
+Both `systemMessage` and `additionalContext` are supported. The `source` field in input (`startup|resume|clear`) allows different injection behavior per trigger.
+      // Inject context via custom tool or tui.prompt.append
+OpenCode uses `experimental.session.compacting` for context that must survive compaction — critical for persistent session awareness.
+For context injection to work, a SessionStart hook needs to query Entire.io's data. Available CLI commands:
+| `entire status` | Active sessions, agent types, token counts | "What's happening now across all agents?" |
+| `entire explain --short` | Checkpoint list with session summaries | "What was accomplished in recent sessions?" |
+| `entire explain --checkpoint <id> --short` | Single checkpoint summary | "What did session X do?" |
+| `entire explain --session <id>` | All checkpoints for a session | "Full history of a specific session" |
+| `entire explain --generate` | AI-generated summary (requires Claude CLI) | "Summarize what happened for injection" |
+- `entire explain --generate`: 3-10s (calls Claude CLI for AI summary)
+**Integration Pattern: SessionStart → entire status → format → inject as context**
+A shell hook can be shared across Claude Code and Gemini CLI (both use shell commands). OpenCode requires a TypeScript wrapper that shells out to the `entire` binary.
+_Source: [Entire CLI Commands](https://docs.entire.io/cli/commands), local testing on this project_
+The core architectural challenge: making each agent aware of what other agents are doing in parallel. The data flow:
+              └→ Injects: "Claude Code session active on branch X, working on Y"
+  2. Filter for sessions on same branch or touching same files
+  3. If overlap detected → inject warning context
+  4. If no overlap → inject awareness context (FYI only)
+  3. Compare against other active sessions' files_touched
+_Source: Architecture derived from [Entire.io Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts) and [Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/)_
+Entire.io's commit trailers create a traceability chain that maps directly to Cohezion's existing BMAD workflow:
+- From checkpoint → `entire explain --checkpoint <id>` → files, prompts, tokens
+- From session → `entire explain --session <id>` → all checkpoints in session

+- Public repos expose full session transcripts

- **Prompt:** LLM evaluation (semantic)
- **Agent:** Deep analysis with tool access

### Gemini CLI Hook System

| `SessionStart` | Session begins | No |

| `BeforeModel` | Before LLM request | **Yes** (modify/mock) |
| `AfterModel` | After LLM response | **Yes** (filter/redact) |
| `BeforeToolSelection` | Before tool selection | **Yes** (filter tools) |
| `BeforeTool` | Before tool execution | **Yes** (validate/block) |
| `AfterTool` | After tool execution | No |
| `PreCompress` | Before context compression | No |
| `Notification` | System notification | No |

**Configuration:** JSON in `.gemini/settings.json` at three levels: project, user (`~/.gemini/settings.json`), system (`/etc/gemini-cli/settings.json`).

**I/O:** JSON via stdin/stdout. Exit code 0 = success, 2 = block, other = warning.

**Environment Variables:** `GEMINI_PROJECT_DIR`, `GEMINI_SESSION_ID`, `GEMINI_CWD`, `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` (compatibility alias).

**Management:** `/hooks panel`, `/hooks enable-all`, `/hooks disable-all`.

**Current Entire.io Integration Status (this project):** **NOT INSTALLED** — `.gemini/` directory exists (commands only) but no `settings.json` with Entire hooks.

_Source: [Google Developers Blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/tailor-gemini-cli-to-your-workflow-with-hooks/), [Gemini CLI Hooks Docs](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/)_

| Session | `session.created`, `session.compacted`, `session.deleted`, `session.diff`, `session.error`, `session.idle`, `session.status`, `session.updated` |

### Configuration Layering

All three CLIs and Entire.io use layered configuration with consistent precedence:

| Layer | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode | Entire.io |
|-------|-------------|------------|----------|-----------|
| **Project** | `.claude/settings.json` | `.gemini/settings.json` | `.opencode/` | `.entire/settings.json` |

_Source: [Entire Configuration](https://docs.entire.io/cli/configuration), respective CLI documentation_

### Technology Adoption Trends

**Agent-Agnostic Tooling:** Entire.io represents a growing trend of agent-agnostic developer tools. Rather than vendor lock-in to Anthropic/Google/OpenCode-specific solutions, Entire stores everything in Git — portable across agents.

**Hook Standardization:** All three CLIs now have hook/extension systems (Claude Code since late 2025, Gemini CLI hooks since v0.26.0 January 2026, OpenCode plugins since launch). The patterns are converging:
- Session lifecycle events
- Tool interception (before/after)
- Context compaction hooks
- Shell command execution model

**Community Ecosystem Growth:** Gemini CLI has 1M+ developers with an extension marketplace. OpenCode has Oh My OpenCode (44 hooks, 26+ tools). Claude Code has plugins and BMAD. This creates opportunities for cross-agent tooling.

**Known Limitations of Entire.io:**
- No retention policy for `entire/checkpoints/v1` (grows forever)
- Squash merges break bidirectional linking (trailers disappear)
- No PR linkage (branch names recorded but no PR number/URL)
- Full transcripts stored in pushable branches (privacy concern for public repos)
- Auto-summarization requires Claude CLI (not agent-agnostic for this feature)

_Source: [Under the Hood article](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/), [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues)_

## Integration Patterns Analysis

### Communication Protocols — Unified stdin/stdout JSON

All three CLIs use a conceptually similar hook communication pattern, but with important differences:

| Aspect | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode |
|--------|-------------|------------|----------|
| **Transport** | stdin → stdout (JSON) | stdin → stdout (JSON) | Function call → return value |
| **Block signal** | Exit 2 OR `permissionDecision: "deny"` | Exit 2 OR `decision: "deny"` | `throw new Error()` |
| **Allow signal** | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Exit 0 (empty stdout) | Return nothing |
| **Context injection** | `additionalContext` field in hookSpecificOutput | `systemMessage` or `additionalContext` | Modify args or return context |
| **Handler types** | Command, HTTP, Prompt, Agent | Command only | TypeScript/JavaScript function |
| **Timeout default** | 60s | 60s | N/A (sync JS execution) |
| **Async support** | Yes (background hooks with later injection) | No | Yes (async functions) |

**Key Insight for Entire.io:** The Entire.io CLI already implements adapter layers per agent. For Claude Code and Gemini CLI, it writes JSON shell command hooks into `settings.json`. For OpenCode, it generates a TypeScript plugin file at `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. This means the protocol translation is handled by Entire.io — consumers don't need to care about per-CLI differences.

_Source: [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Gemini CLI Hooks Reference](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/reference/), [OpenCode Plugins Docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/)_

### Hook Event Mapping Across CLIs

Entire.io needs to map its 7 lifecycle events to each CLI's event model:

| Entire.io Hook | Claude Code Event | Gemini CLI Event | OpenCode Event |
|----------------|-------------------|------------------|----------------|
| `SessionStart` | `SessionStart` | `SessionStart` | `session.created` |
| `SessionEnd` | `SessionEnd` | `SessionEnd` | `session.idle` or `session.deleted` |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | `UserPromptSubmit` | `BeforeAgent` | `tui.command.execute` |
| `Stop` (checkpoint trigger) | `Stop` | `AfterAgent` | `session.updated` |
| `PreToolUse` (subagent) | `PreToolUse` (matcher: `Agent`) | `BeforeTool` | `tool.execute.before` |
| `PostToolUse` (subagent) | `PostToolUse` (matcher: `Agent`) | `AfterTool` | `tool.execute.after` |
| `PostToolUse[TodoWrite]` | `PostToolUse` (matcher: `TodoWrite`) | `AfterTool` (matcher: `todo`) | `todo.updated` |

**Confidence: HIGH for Claude Code (GA), MEDIUM for Gemini/OpenCode (preview)**

_Source: [Under the Hood article](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/), respective CLI documentation_

### Context Injection Patterns — The Key Integration Point

The most valuable pattern for Cohezion's agent context awareness is **SessionStart context injection**. Each CLI supports injecting context when a session starts:

**Claude Code:**
```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "Context string injected into Claude's system prompt"
  }
}
```
The `additionalContext` is prepended to the first prompt. Non-JSON stdout from SessionStart hooks is also injected directly into context.

**Gemini CLI:**
```json
{
  "systemMessage": "Context injected as system message",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "additionalContext": "Additional context appended to prompt"
  }
}
```
Both `systemMessage` and `additionalContext` are supported. The `source` field in input (`startup|resume|clear`) allows different injection behavior per trigger.

**OpenCode:**
```typescript
export const ContextPlugin = async ({ project }) => ({
  hooks: {
    "session.created": async (input) => {
      // Inject context via custom tool or tui.prompt.append
    },
    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input) => {
      // Inject context that survives compaction
    }
  }
})
```
OpenCode uses `experimental.session.compacting` for context that must survive compaction — critical for persistent session awareness.

_Source: [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Gemini CLI Hooks Reference](https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/reference/), [OpenCode Plugins](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/)_

### Entire.io Data Access Patterns

For context injection to work, a SessionStart hook needs to query Entire.io's data. Available CLI commands:

| Command | Output | Use Case |
|---------|--------|----------|
| `entire status` | Active sessions, agent types, token counts | "What's happening now across all agents?" |
| `entire explain --short` | Checkpoint list with session summaries | "What was accomplished in recent sessions?" |
| `entire explain --checkpoint <id> --short` | Single checkpoint summary | "What did session X do?" |
| `entire explain --session <id>` | All checkpoints for a session | "Full history of a specific session" |
| `entire explain --generate` | AI-generated summary (requires Claude CLI) | "Summarize what happened for injection" |

**Performance Characteristics:**
- `entire status`: ~200ms (reads local metadata)
- `entire explain --short`: ~500ms (reads checkpoint branch)
- `entire explain --generate`: 3-10s (calls Claude CLI for AI summary)
- `entire rewind --list`: ~300ms (reads shadow branches)

**Integration Pattern: SessionStart → entire status → format → inject as context**

A shell hook can be shared across Claude Code and Gemini CLI (both use shell commands). OpenCode requires a TypeScript wrapper that shells out to the `entire` binary.

_Source: [Entire CLI Commands](https://docs.entire.io/cli/commands), local testing on this project_

### Cross-Agent Session Visibility Architecture

The core architectural challenge: making each agent aware of what other agents are doing in parallel. The data flow:

```
Agent A (Claude Code) starts session
  └→ Entire hooks capture SessionStart
      └→ Shadow branch created
          └→ Checkpoints accumulate on turns

Agent B (Gemini CLI) starts session
  └→ SessionStart hook fires
      └→ Hook runs: entire status
          └→ Sees Agent A's active session
              └→ Injects: "Claude Code session active on branch X, working on Y"
```

**Conflict Detection Pattern:**
```
SessionStart hook:
  1. Run `entire status` → parse JSON output
  2. Filter for sessions on same branch or touching same files
  3. If overlap detected → inject warning context
  4. If no overlap → inject awareness context (FYI only)
```

**File-Level Conflict Detection (Advanced):**
```
Stop/AfterAgent hook:
  1. Run `entire explain --checkpoint <latest> --short`
  2. Extract files_touched list
  3. Compare against other active sessions' files_touched
  4. If overlap → inject merge-risk warning
```

_Source: Architecture derived from [Entire.io Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts) and [Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/)_

### Bidirectional Traceability Integration

Entire.io's commit trailers create a traceability chain that maps directly to Cohezion's existing BMAD workflow:

```
PRD Requirement (FR-X)
  └→ Epic (Epic 12: Sovereign-Sync Bedrock)
      └→ Story (Story 12.1: JSON-RPC Bridge)
          └→ Sprint Task (implementation)
              └→ Git Commit (feat: add JSON-RPC gateway)
                  └→ Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7
                      └→ Full Session Transcript
                          └→ Prompts, Decisions, Files, Token Cost
```

**Trailer Format:**
```
feat: add JSON-RPC gateway

Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7
Entire-Attribution: 73% agent (146/200 lines)
```

**Querying the chain:**
- From commit → `entire explain --commit <sha>` → session context
- From checkpoint → `entire explain --checkpoint <id>` → files, prompts, tokens
- From session → `entire explain --session <id>` → all checkpoints in session

**Known Limitation:** Squash merges (common in PR workflows) destroy commit trailers, breaking the bidirectional link. This needs a workaround for Cohezion's worktree-based `cz worktree sync` flow.

_Source: [Core Concepts](https://docs.entire.io/core-concepts), [Under the Hood](https://julien.danjou.info/blog/how-entire-works-under-the-hood/)_

### Security Patterns

**Secret Redaction:** Entire.io performs best-effort redaction of API keys, tokens, and credentials when writing to `entire/checkpoints/v1`. However:
- Shadow branches during active sessions may contain unredacted data
- Redaction is pattern-based, not comprehensive
- Public repos expose full session transcripts

**Hook Security:**
- Claude Code: Hooks run with user permissions, outside the Bash tool sandbox
- Gemini CLI: Project-level hooks fingerprinted; warns on changes from git pull
- OpenCode: Plugin hooks don't intercept subagent tool calls (known bug — [Issue #5894](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/5894))

**Recommendation for Cohezion:** Since Cohezion is a private repo with sensitive research data:
1. Use `.entire/settings.local.json` for any API keys in summarization config
2. Review `entire/checkpoints/v1` before pushing to remote
3. Consider `--skip-push-sessions` for sensitive branches

_Source: [GitHub README](https://github.com/entireio/cli), [Entire Configuration](https://docs.entire.io/cli/configuration)_

### Current State Gap Analysis (This Project)

| Component | Expected | Actual | Gap |
|-----------|----------|--------|-----|
| Claude Code hooks | Full lifecycle | **Installed** (6 event types) | None |
| Gemini CLI hooks | Full lifecycle | **Missing** (no `.gemini/settings.json`) | `entire enable --agent gemini` needed |
| OpenCode plugin | TypeScript plugin | **Missing** (no `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`) | `entire enable --agent opencode` needed |
| Context injection | SessionStart hook queries `entire status` | **Not implemented** | Custom hook needed per CLI |
| Cross-session awareness | Agents see each other's work | **Not implemented** | Custom SessionStart hook + formatter |
| Conflict detection | File-level overlap warnings | **Not implemented** | Custom Stop/AfterAgent hook |
| Traceability | Commit trailers → BMAD stories | **Passive** (trailers exist but not queried) | Query integration with sprint status |
| Stuck session cleanup | Automated | **Manual** (15 stuck sessions) | `entire doctor --force` or automated cron |

_Confidence: HIGH — verified against local installation state_

### The Cross-Runtime Problem

GSD solves the cross-runtime problem for AI coding agent tools. Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot: each runtime defines its own format for commands, agents, and configuration. Supporting a second means maintaining a parallel copy of every file. Supporting three means triple the maintenance burden, and the formats inevitably drift.

### GSD's Architectural Approach

What makes GSD's approach particularly noteworthy is its decision to build an independent installer rather than relying on Claude Code's plugin system. While GSD predates Claude Code's plugin architecture and agent skills specification, the project deliberately maintains its own installation and conversion pipeline. This architectural choice enables GSD to adapt Claude Code's subagent and command formats to work seamlessly with both Gemini CLI and OpenCode — runtimes that have no equivalent plugin mechanism.

The installer acts as a translation layer, transforming a single canonical codebase into three runtime-specific deployments, each with its own file structure, naming conventions, and tool vocabularies.

The solution: author everything once in Claude Code format, then convert at install time.

### What GSD Ships

GSD (Get "Stuff" Done) is a spec-driven development system designed to help AI coding agents maintain context and productivity across long development sessions. It provides a structured framework for tracking specifications, bugs, todos, milestones, and project requirements — all the essential elements that prevent context rot when working with AI assistants.

The project ships 11 specialized agents, a full set of slash commands, workflow definitions, templates, and hooks.

### Adoption

GSD is used by engineers at Amazon, Google, Shopify, and Webflow. The multi-runtime installer is how those teams standardize on GSD regardless of which AI coding agent they prefer.

---

- **GitHub repo**: https://github.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done — A light-weight and powerful meta-prompting, context engineering and spec-driven development system for Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and Codex.

The installer performs runtime-specific transformations. The installer handles: runtime selection, location selection, file copying, transformation (applying runtime-specific format changes like OpenCode flattening and Gemini TOML conversion), and configuration.

- **Installation details** (https://zread.ai/gsd-build/get-shit-done/3-installation-guide): OpenCode is an open-source alternative that supports free models. GSD automatically converts Claude Code formats for OpenCode compatibility. Gemini CLI provides access to Google's AI models. GSD adapts its agent system for Gemini's requirements.

- **OpenCode community port** (https://github.com/rokicool/gsd-opencode): The original GSD was adapted for OpenCode by rokicool and enthusiasts, and later TÂCHES decided to include support for OpenCode in their own product.

- **npm package** (`get-shit-done-cc`): OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and Codex are now natively supported via `npx get-shit-done-cc`.

- **Claude Code as reference runtime** (DeepWiki): Claude Code is the primary runtime target for GSD and serves as the reference implementation. The codebase structure in the repository mirrors the Claude Code format, which means minimal transformation is required during installation.

Here are the key findings on **cross-agent context sharing architecture and agentic CLI tools coordination patterns** in 2026:

---

## Emerging Protocols for Cross-Agent Context Sharing

The landscape is rapidly evolving around several standardized protocols:

- LLM-powered autonomous agents demand robust, standardized protocols to integrate tools, share contextual data, and coordinate tasks across heterogeneous systems. Ad-hoc integrations are difficult to scale, secure, and generalize across domains. A survey on arXiv examines four emerging agent communication protocols: **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, **Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)**, **Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A)**, and **Agent Network Protocol (ANP)**, each addressing interoperability in distinct deployment contexts.

- MCP provided a vital mechanism for standardizing how agents share context and coordinate within a single multi-agent system, addressing the "context bottleneck" by allowing specialized agents to maintain a shared understanding of a task. Yet, a fundamental gap remains: there is no universal protocol that allows an agent built on one platform to securely discover and collaborate with an agent on another.

- ACP is designed to be the "TCP/IP of the Agentic Web," providing the necessary layers for discovery, transport, and semantic alignment.

## Core Coordination Patterns

Several canonical patterns have emerged for multi-agent coordination:

1. **Sequential/Pipeline Pattern**: The sequential orchestration pattern chains AI agents in a predefined, linear order. Each agent processes the output from the previous agent in the sequence, creating a pipeline of specialized transformations.

2. **Hub-and-Spoke / Orchestrator-Worker**: One agent acts as a decision maker, receiving requests and dispatching them to specialized agents. The coordinator maintains context and synthesizes results. Perfect for customer service systems where a routing agent directs queries to specialists.

3. **Group Chat / Roundtable**: The group chat orchestration pattern enables multiple agents to solve problems, make decisions, or validate work by participating in a shared conversation thread. A chat manager coordinates the flow by determining which agents can respond next. Also known as: roundtable, collaborative, multi-agent debate, council.

4. **Parallel/Fan-out**: Multiple agents work simultaneously on independent tasks. A research system might query three data sources at once instead of sequentially. This pattern cuts processing time by 60-80% for tasks with no dependencies between steps.

## Context Management as the Critical Layer

- When it comes to coordination between a multi-agent AI system, context is king. Without it, even the most sophisticated agents can duplicate work, contradict one another and overlook critical constraints. Effective context management enables agents to maintain shared awareness of common goals, peer activities, task histories, and status.

- A comprehensive framework for advancing multi-agent systems through MCP addresses challenges through standardized context sharing and coordination mechanisms, developing a unified theoretical foundation, advanced context management techniques, and scalable coordination patterns.

## Architectural Models

- Multi-agent AI systems typically use two architectural models: **Hierarchical**, where a lead agent orchestrates specialized sub-agents, and **Peer-to-peer**, where agents work collaboratively without a direct point of control but require robust communication protocols. For most enterprises, hybrid models work best.

## Agentic Coding & CLI Tools in 2026

- Multi-agent architectures use an orchestrator to coordinate specialized agents working in parallel—each with dedicated context—then synthesize results into integrated output.

- In 2025, agentic AI changed how a large swath of developers write code. 2026 is poised to be the year when the systemic effects of this evolutionary shift reconfigure the software development lifecycle.

- Flow engineering is the discipline of designing the control flow, state transitions, and decision boundaries around LLM calls rather than optimizing the calls themselves. It treats agent construction as a software architecture problem.

## Key Frameworks

Leading frameworks include **LangGraph** (graph-based workflows), **MetaGPT** (role-based collaboration for software development), **AutoGen** (conversational planner–executor–critic loops), **CrewAI** (role-specific agent "crews"), and **Agents SDK by OpenAI** (lightweight orchestration with function calling).

---

The overall trend in 2026 is a shift from single-agent systems to coordinated multi-agent architectures, with MCP and related protocols serving as the backbone for cross-agent context sharing, and production systems increasingly composing multiple coordination patterns together. Agent-to-agent communication is identified as where most projects fail, making robust context-sharing protocols the key differentiator for successful deployments.

Here are the search results covering **git hooks**, **observer pattern architecture**, **multi-agent session coordination**, and **design patterns** (with a 2026 focus):

---

## 1. Git Hooks in Multi-Agent Coordination

Long-running agents need new infrastructure: observability into what agents are doing, hooks for human review, and graceful degradation when things go wrong. Specifically, Claude Code uses stop hooks to verify work after each iteration and the Ralph Loop tracks progress via git history. However, there are no standards for agent observability, common debugging interfaces, or agreed-upon patterns for human-in-the-loop monitoring.

Anthropic described one version of the Ralph loop where an initializer agent sets up an environment (e.g., a plan file, a tracking file) and sub-agents tackle individual tasks from the plan file.

---

## 2. Observer Pattern in Agent Architectures

The observer pattern is a software design pattern in which an object, called the subject, maintains a list of its dependents, called observers, and notifies them automatically of any state changes, usually by calling one of their methods.

In the context of multi-agent systems, observable coordination means parents monitor children through reactive patterns. Microsoft's Azure architecture guide notes that several orchestration patterns support human-in-the-loop (HITL) involvement: observers in group chat, reviewers in maker-checker loops, and escalation targets in handoff and magentic orchestrations.

Mandatory gates make the orchestration synchronous at that step, so persist state at these checkpoints to allow resumption without replaying prior agent work.

---

## 3. Multi-Agent Session Coordination Design Patterns (2026)

### Agentic Design Patterns (SitePoint, 2026)

The skill set required combines traditional software engineering fundamentals, including state management, error handling, concurrency control, and observability, with an understanding of LLM capabilities and limitations. These patterns are not mutually exclusive; production systems routinely compose two or three together. Each pattern addresses a different aspect of agent behavior, from self-correction to multi-agent coordination.

A slight variation of the sequential pipeline is the coordinator/dispatcher pattern, in which one agent acts as a decision maker, receiving a request and dispatching it to a specialized agent further down the line. # GSD Cross-Runtime Translation Architecture

## Overview

GSD maintains a **single canonical format** (Claude Code native) and transforms it during installation for OpenCode and Gemini CLI compatibility. The installer (`bin/install.js`) acts as the translation layer.

## Canonical Format (Claude Code)

The source format features:
- **Commands**: Nested structure (`commands/gsd/debug/start.md`)
- **Frontmatter**: YAML with `allowed-tools: [...]` array syntax
- **Tool names**: PascalCase (`AskUserQuestion`, `SlashCommand`, `Read`, `Write`)
- **Configuration**: `settings.json` in `~/.claude/`

## OpenCode Transformation Pipeline

### 1. Command Structure Flattening

Nested command hierarchy becomes flat:
- Source: `commands/gsd/debug/start.md`
- Target: `command/gsd-debug-start.md`

Implementation via `copyFlattenedCommands()` recursively traverses nested directories and renames files with hyphen-separated paths.

### 2. Tool Name Mapping

Critical remapping occurs:

| Canonical | OpenCode |
|-----------|----------|
| `AskUserQuestion` | `question` |
| `SlashCommand` | `skill` |
| `TodoWrite` | `todowrite` |
| `Read` → `read`, `Write` → `write` |

The mapper in lines 286-327 normalizes tool names to OpenCode's lowercase convention while preserving functionality.

### 3. Frontmatter Restructuring

```yaml
# Canonical
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Write

# OpenCode
tools:
  read: true
  write: true
```

The `convertClaudeToOpencodeFrontmatter()` function transforms array-based tool declarations into object-based permission maps.

### 4. Color Code Conversion

Named colors convert to hex:
- `cyan` → `#00FFFF`
- `red` → `#FF0000`

This ensures terminal/UI compatibility across runtimes.

### 5. Automatic Permission Grants

The installer modifies `opencode.json` to pre-authorize GSD operations:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "read": {"~/.config/opencode/get-shit-done": "always"},
    "external_directory": {"~/.config/opencode/get-shit-done/bin": "always"}
  }
}
```

This prevents permission prompts during execution. Implementation: lines 1034-1087.

## Gemini CLI Transformation Pipeline

### 1. Markdown to TOML Conversion

Entire files restructure:

```toml
description = "Execute a phase plan"
prompt = "Your task is to execute tasks from the plan..."
```

The `convertClaudeToGeminiToml()` extracts frontmatter and body separately, converting YAML to TOML equivalents.

### 2. Tool Name Normalization

Gemini uses snake_case with semantic prefixes:

| Canonical | Gemini |
|-----------|--------|
| `Read` | `read_file` |
| `Write` | `write_file` |
| `Bash` | `run_shell_command` |
| `AskUserQuestion` | `ask_user` |

### 3. MCP Tool Exclusion

Tools matching `mcp__*` pattern are stripped from frontmatter because Gemini auto-discovers these from the `mcpServers` configuration at runtime. The `Task` tool is also excluded since agents become callable tools automatically.

### 4. HTML Tag Stripping

Terminal compatibility requires converting rich formatting:
- `<sub>text</sub>` → `*(text)*`
- `<sup>text</sup>` → `^(text)^`

This ensures prompts render correctly in terminal environments where HTML is unsupported.

## Installation Flow Diagram

```
npx get-shit-done-cc [flags]
    ↓
[Runtime Detection: --claude / --opencode / --gemini / --all]
    ↓
[Scope Selection: --global / --local]
    ↓
[Directory Resolution (env vars, XDG compliance)]
    ↓
    ├─→ Claude Code: Copy unchanged to ~/.claude/
    │
    ├─→ OpenCode: 
    │    • Flatten commands
    │    • Map tool names (PascalCase → lowercase)
    │    • Convert frontmatter (array → object)
    │    • Convert colors (named → hex)
    │    • Grant permissions in opencode.json
    │    → Deploy to ~/.config/opencode/
    │
    └─→ Gemini CLI:
         • Convert markdown → TOML
         • Normalize tool names (→ snake_case)
         • Strip MCP/Task tools
         • Remove HTML tags
         → Deploy to ~/.gemini/
    ↓
[Register hooks in settings.json]
    ↓
[Installation complete]
```

## Key Implementation Details

### Config Directory Resolution Priority

**Claude Code**:
1. `--config-dir` flag
2. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` env var
3. `~/.claude` (default)

**OpenCode** (XDG-compliant):
1. `--config-dir` flag
2. `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` env var
3. `XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode` if set
4. `~/.config/opencode` (XDG default)

**Gemini CLI**:
1. `--config-dir` flag
2. `GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR` env var
3. `~/.gemini` (default)

### Preservation of Local Modifications

The patch system (`commands/gsd/reapply-patches.md`) preserves customizations across updates by tracking diffs between versions and reapplying them after installation completes.

### Version Tracking

Installed version stored in `get-shit-done/VERSION` enables:
- Update detection (comparing current vs. latest)
- Patch compatibility verification
- Hook version compatibility checks

## Multi-Runtime Deployment Result

A single source repository deploys identically to all three runtimes through deterministic transformation rules, ensuring unified GSD behavior while respecting each runtime's architectural constraints and naming conventions.

## Architectural Patterns and Design

### Recommended System Architecture: Observer-Mediated Hub-and-Spoke

After analyzing multi-agent coordination patterns, the architecture that best fits Cohezion's Entire.io integration is a **hub-and-spoke pattern with observer-mediated context sharing**, where Entire.io serves as the hub and each agent CLI is a spoke.

```
                    ┌──────────────────────┐
                    │   Entire.io Hub      │
                    │  (Git Shadow Branch)  │
                    │  entire/checkpoints   │
                    │  /v1 metadata         │
                    └──────┬───────────────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────────┐
              │            │                │
    ┌─────────▼──┐  ┌─────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼─────┐
    │ Claude Code │  │ Gemini CLI │  │  OpenCode  │
    │   Hooks     │  │   Hooks    │  │  Plugin    │
    │ (JSON cmd)  │  │ (JSON cmd) │  │ (TS func)  │
    └─────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘
```

**Why this pattern over alternatives:**

| Pattern | Fit | Reason |
|---------|-----|--------|
| Hub-and-Spoke (Entire.io as hub) | **Best** | Entire.io already acts as centralized session store; agents don't need to talk directly to each other |
| Peer-to-Peer (agents talk directly) | Poor | No agent-to-agent protocol exists; CLIs don't know about each other |
| Blackboard (shared memory space) | Medium | Git shadow branches are a blackboard, but too slow for real-time coordination |
| Orchestrator-Worker | Poor | No single agent coordinates others; all agents are independent |

**Key architectural insight:** We don't need agents to communicate with each other in real-time. We need each agent to be **aware of what other agents have done and are doing** when it starts. This is a read-only context injection problem, not a bidirectional communication problem. Entire.io's existing `entire status` command provides the data; we just need hooks to inject it.

_Source: [Google's Multi-Agent Patterns (InfoQ)](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/01/multi-agent-design-patterns/), [Microsoft Multi-Agent Reference Architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-reference-architecture/docs/reference-architecture/Patterns.html), [Event-Driven Multi-Agent Systems (Confluent)](https://www.confluent.io/blog/event-driven-multi-agent-systems/)_

### Cross-Runtime Translation Pattern (Lessons from GSD)

The [GSD project](https://github.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done) (used at Amazon, Google, Shopify, Webflow) solved the exact same cross-runtime problem: one codebase targeting Claude Code, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI. Their architecture provides a proven pattern:

**Canonical Format + Install-Time Transformation:**
```
Canonical (Claude Code format)
    ↓
[Runtime Detector]
    ├→ Claude Code: Copy unchanged to ~/.claude/
    ├→ OpenCode: Flatten commands, map tools, convert frontmatter → ~/.config/opencode/
    └→ Gemini CLI: Convert MD→TOML, normalize tools, strip MCP → ~/.gemini/
```

**Key Transformations Required:**

| Aspect | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode |
|--------|-------------|------------|----------|
| Hook format | JSON in `settings.json` | JSON in `settings.json` | TypeScript in `plugins/` |
| Tool names | PascalCase (`Read`, `Write`) | snake_case (`read_file`, `write_file`) | lowercase (`read`, `write`) |
| Command structure | Nested dirs | TOML files | Flat files |
| Config location | `~/.claude/` | `~/.gemini/` | `~/.config/opencode/` |

**Relevance to Cohezion:** Entire.io already implements per-agent adapters (JSON for Claude/Gemini, TypeScript for OpenCode). Our custom context injection hooks should follow the same pattern — write the logic once in a shell script, then wrap it for each runtime.

_Source: [GSD Architecture (DeepWiki)](https://deepwiki.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done), [One Codebase Three Runtimes (Rick Hightower)](https://medium.com/@richardhightower/one-codebase-three-runtimes-how-gsd-targets-claude-code-opencode-and-gemini-cli-29c98cfe96c6)_

### Context Injection Architecture

The core architectural component is a **SessionStart context injector** — a hook/plugin that runs when any agent starts a session and injects awareness of parallel sessions.

**Proposed Architecture:**

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SessionStart Hook (shared shell script)              │
│                                                      │
│  1. entire status --quiet → parse active sessions    │
│  2. Filter: same branch? same files? conflicts?      │
│  3. Format: concise context string                   │
│  4. Return: JSON with additionalContext               │
└──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                   │
     ┌─────────────┼─────────────────────┐
     │             │                     │
┌────▼────┐  ┌────▼────┐  ┌─────────────▼──────────┐
│ Claude  │  │ Gemini  │  │ OpenCode               │
│ Hook    │  │ Hook    │  │ Plugin                  │
│ wrapper │  │ wrapper │  │ wrapper                 │
│ (JSON)  │  │ (JSON)  │  │ (TS → shell out)       │
└─────────┘  └─────────┘  └────────────────────────┘
```

**Three-layer design:**

1. **Core Logic Layer** (`entire-context.sh`): A single shell script that queries `entire status`, formats context, and outputs JSON. Agent-agnostic — pure data transformation.

2. **Adapter Layer** (per-CLI wrappers):
   - Claude Code: Shell hook in `.claude/settings.json` that calls `entire-context.sh` and returns `{ hookSpecificOutput: { additionalContext: "..." } }`
   - Gemini CLI: Shell hook in `.gemini/settings.json` that calls `entire-context.sh` and returns `{ systemMessage: "..." }`

## Architectural Patterns and Design

### Recommended System Architecture: Observer-Mediated Hub-and-Spoke

After analyzing multi-agent coordination patterns, the architecture that best fits Cohezion's Entire.io integration is a **hub-and-spoke pattern with observer-mediated context sharing**, where Entire.io serves as the hub and each agent CLI is a spoke.

```
                    ┌──────────────────────┐
                    │   Entire.io Hub      │
                    │  (Git Shadow Branch)  │
                    │  entire/checkpoints   │
                    │  /v1 metadata         │
                    └──────┬───────────────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────────┐
              │            │                │
    ┌─────────▼──┐  ┌─────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼─────┐
    │ Claude Code │  │ Gemini CLI │  │  OpenCode  │
    │   Hooks     │  │   Hooks    │  │  Plugin    │
    │ (JSON cmd)  │  │ (JSON cmd) │  │ (TS func)  │
    └─────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘
```

**Why this pattern over alternatives:**

| Pattern | Fit | Reason |
|---------|-----|--------|
| Hub-and-Spoke (Entire.io as hub) | **Best** | Entire.io already acts as centralized session store; agents don't need to talk directly to each other |
| Peer-to-Peer (agents talk directly) | Poor | No agent-to-agent protocol exists; CLIs don't know about each other |
| Blackboard (shared memory space) | Medium | Git shadow branches are a blackboard, but too slow for real-time coordination |
| Orchestrator-Worker | Poor | No single agent coordinates others; all agents are independent |

**Key architectural insight:** We don't need agents to communicate with each other in real-time. We need each agent to be **aware of what other agents have done and are doing** when it starts. This is a read-only context injection problem, not a bidirectional communication problem. Entire.io's existing `entire status` command provides the data; we just need hooks to inject it.

_Source: [Google's Multi-Agent Patterns (InfoQ)](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/01/multi-agent-design-patterns/), [Microsoft Multi-Agent Reference Architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-reference-architecture/docs/reference-architecture/Patterns.html), [Event-Driven Multi-Agent Systems (Confluent)](https://www.confluent.io/blog/event-driven-multi-agent-systems/)_

### Cross-Runtime Translation Pattern (Lessons from GSD)

The [GSD project](https://github.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done) (used at Amazon, Google, Shopify, Webflow) solved the exact same cross-runtime problem: one codebase targeting Claude Code, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI. Their architecture provides a proven pattern:

**Canonical Format + Install-Time Transformation:**
```
Canonical (Claude Code format)
    ↓
[Runtime Detector]
    ├→ Claude Code: Copy unchanged to ~/.claude/
    ├→ OpenCode: Flatten commands, map tools, convert frontmatter → ~/.config/opencode/
    └→ Gemini CLI: Convert MD→TOML, normalize tools, strip MCP → ~/.gemini/
```

**Key Transformations Required:**

| Aspect | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | OpenCode |
|--------|-------------|------------|----------|
| Hook format | JSON in `settings.json` | JSON in `settings.json` | TypeScript in `plugins/` |
| Tool names | PascalCase (`Read`, `Write`) | snake_case (`read_file`, `write_file`) | lowercase (`read`, `write`) |
| Command structure | Nested dirs | TOML files | Flat files |
| Config location | `~/.claude/` | `~/.gemini/` | `~/.config/opencode/` |

**Relevance to Cohezion:** Entire.io already implements per-agent adapters (JSON for Claude/Gemini, TypeScript for OpenCode). Our custom context injection hooks should follow the same pattern — write the logic once in a shell script, then wrap it for each runtime.

_Source: [GSD Architecture (DeepWiki)](https://deepwiki.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done), [One Codebase Three Runtimes (Rick Hightower)](https://medium.com/@richardhightower/one-codebase-three-runtimes-how-gsd-targets-claude-code-opencode-and-gemini-cli-29c98cfe96c6)_

The core architectural component is a **SessionStart context injector** — a hook/plugin that runs when any agent starts a session and injects awareness of parallel sessions.

**Proposed Architecture:**

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SessionStart Hook (shared shell script)              │
│                                                      │
│  1. entire status --quiet → parse active sessions    │
│  2. Filter: same branch? same files? conflicts?      │
│  3. Format: concise context string                   │
│  4. Return: JSON with additionalContext               │
└──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                   │
     ┌─────────────┼─────────────────────┐
     │             │                     │
┌────▼────┐  ┌────▼────┐  ┌─────────────▼──────────┐
│ Claude  │  │ Gemini  │  │ OpenCode               │
│ Hook    │  │ Hook    │  │ Plugin                  │
│ wrapper │  │ wrapper │  │ wrapper                 │
│ (JSON)  │  │ (JSON)  │  │ (TS → shell out)       │
└─────────┘  └─────────┘  └────────────────────────┘
```

## Technical Research Scope Confirmation

**Research Topic:** Entire.io Cross-Agent Integration for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode
**Research Goals:** Understand Entire.io architecture, cross-CLI integration model, hook points per agent, and how to build automated context injection — informing PRD/Architecture/Epics updates for full traceability

**Technical Research Scope:**

- Architecture Analysis - Entire.io checkpoint/shadow-branch/session model, data storage format, agent CLI detection
- Implementation Approaches - Hook integration patterns per CLI, shared session state formats
- Technology Stack - Entire.io CLI (Go), shadow git branches, checkpoint JSONL, AI summaries, CLI hook/extension APIs
